Containers

1. Containers

HarborWorks can package the status site’s runtime in a container, but the host remains responsible for security, storage, networking, and supervision. A container is not a miniature universe in which administrative consequences disappear. This chapter treats it as an ordinary process with explicit isolation and packaging mechanisms.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — Chapter 26 — Containers

2. Container isolation is a set of boundaries

Container processes share a host kernel. Image version, privilege, resource limits and data placement must each be explicit. Replacing a container discards state that was written only to its ephemeral layer.

SOURCE: Container isolation is a set of boundaries

3. Chapter 26 — Containers

HarborWorks can package the status site’s runtime in a container, but the host remains responsible for security, storage, networking, and supervision. A container is not a miniature universe in which administrative consequences disappear. This chapter treats it as an ordinary process with explicit isolation and packaging mechanisms.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — Chapter 26 — Containers

4. 26.1 Containers vs. Virtual Machines

A conventional Linux container shares the host kernel while using isolation mechanisms to provide separate views and controls. A VM runs a guest kernel against virtual hardware. Containers often start quickly and package applications compactly, but kernel compatibility and the host trust boundary remain important.

Choose from workload requirements. A need for a different guest kernel or stronger separation can favor a VM or another isolation technology. A reproducible userspace application with controlled host integration may fit a container well.

Neither choice provides high availability by itself. A container restarted on one failed disk cannot recover data that existed only on that disk. Packaging, orchestration, persistence, and disaster recovery are separate decisions.

Linux example — 26.1

Inspect a container's isolation settings using an existing lab container.

What to check: Containers share the host kernel; inspect mount and resource boundaries rather than assuming VM isolation.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.1 Containers vs. Virtual Machines

6. 26.2 Namespaces

Namespaces give processes different views of selected system resources, such as process IDs, mounts, networking, and user identities. A process can see PID 1 inside its namespace while having another PID from the host’s perspective.

Isolation is selective. Sharing the host network namespace removes a network boundary; bind-mounting host directories exposes those paths. User namespaces can map identities differently between container and host. “Root inside” is not a complete statement without those mappings and privileges.

Diagnose from the relevant view. A listener visible inside a container may not be published on the host. A file path inside the image may be hidden by a runtime volume mount. Inspect the actual runtime configuration rather than the Containerfile alone.

Linux example — 26.2

Read namespace identities of the current shell.

What to check: Namespace links identify isolation objects, not a full security guarantee.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.2 Namespaces

8. 26.3 Control Groups

Control groups account for and control groups of processes. Container runtimes use them to implement resource policies where the host and permissions support those controls. A CPU quota limits time allocation; a memory ceiling can trigger a container-scoped failure before the host is globally full.

Set limits from tests, not aesthetics. Too-small memory limits can make an otherwise correct application repeatedly fail; no limits can allow one workload to harm its neighbors. Observe throttling, pressure, and termination events alongside application behavior.

On rootless systems, available control depends on cgroup version and delegation. A command accepting a resource option is not sufficient evidence that the intended policy is enforced. Inspect the effective runtime and measure behavior in a lab. (R16)

Linux example — 26.3

Inspect container resource usage without an endless display.

What to check: Limits and current use are different; empty output may simply mean no running containers.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.3 Control Groups

10. 26.4 Container Images

An image describes filesystem layers and runtime defaults. A running container adds writable state and selected mounts. Replacing the container does not necessarily preserve changes made only in its writable layer.

Tags are names that can move to different image content. A digest identifies particular content, subject to platform-manifest details. For reproducible deployment, record the resolved digest, architecture, build inputs, and configuration. A digest proves content identity, not that the image is trustworthy or free of vulnerabilities.

Keep secrets out of build layers. Deleting a secret in a later layer does not reliably remove it from earlier published layers. Use approved build-time secret facilities and runtime secret delivery instead of copying credentials into an image.

Linux example — 26.4

List locally stored images.

What to check: Tags can move; digests identify particular content.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.4 Container Images

12. 26.5 Registries

A registry distributes images and associated metadata. Use fully qualified references to avoid ambiguous short-name resolution. Authenticate through approved tooling, verify transport trust, and protect registry credentials.

Decide what happens when the registry is unavailable during recovery. Pre-pulling a reviewed image or maintaining an approved internal mirror can reduce a dependency, but cached content still needs lifecycle management and security review.

Distinguish scanning, signatures, and provenance. A scan reports selected known issues under its current database. Signature verification checks an identity or policy attached to an artifact. Provenance describes its build history under a trust model. None replaces testing the application and its privileges.

Linux example — 26.5

Inspect configured registry policy.

What to check: User overrides may also exist; verify source and trust before pulling images.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.5 Registries

14. 26.6 Docker Concepts

Docker commonly uses a client communicating with an engine that manages images, containers, networks, and volumes. Access to a powerful daemon socket can permit operations with host-level consequences. Do not treat membership in a Docker administration group as a harmless convenience for untrusted users.

A Dockerfile describes build steps, while the run configuration determines mounts, ports, identities, capabilities, and resource limits. A secure-looking Dockerfile can be undermined by --privileged or by mounting the host root filesystem at runtime.

Rootless operation is a separate supported arrangement with its own prerequisites and limitations. Review the installed engine’s security documentation rather than assuming every Docker installation has identical privilege boundaries. (R57)

Linux example — 26.6

On a Docker lab host, inspect the client and running containers.

What to check: Docker daemon access can confer substantial host privilege; use the approved account setup.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.6 Docker Concepts

16. 26.7 Podman

Podman manages OCI containers and images and supports rootless operation. Ordinary user’s containers and root’s containers normally belong to different storage and management contexts. Switching to sudo podman can appear to make a container disappear because you changed the context.

These observations establish the current environment. Review output before sharing because it can reveal host details and registry information. Check installed version and cgroup support before using examples from newer upstream documentation.

Podman can integrate container lifecycle with systemd. That integration should replace a deliberate supervision design, not be combined blindly with several competing restart mechanisms. (R56)

Linux example — 26.7

Inspect Podman configuration and runtime facts.

What to check: Rootless and privileged invocations have different storage and container inventories.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.7 Podman

19. 26.8 Building Images

A reproducible build starts from reviewed inputs and a defined build context. Files in the context can be sent to the builder even when they are not ultimately copied into the image. Keep private keys, repository secrets, and unrelated large trees out of it.

An illustrative Containerfile for an approved, NGINX-compatible unprivileged base is:

The base must be selected and verified by the operator. It must serve the documented directory on port 8080 as a non-root user for the following lab. The file deliberately does not claim that any arbitrary image will satisfy that contract.

Build with an explicit reference such as podman build --build-arg BASE_IMAGE="$BASE_IMAGE" -t localhost/harbor-status:lab .. A tag named lab is a local convenience; record the image ID or digest used for the actual test.

22. 26.9 Running Containers

A run operation combines an image with runtime policy. Select the container name, user, mounts, port mapping, resource limits, and shutdown behavior explicitly. A detached process still needs a log and supervision plan.

For an approved image that already meets the unprivileged NGINX contract:

This publishes only on host loopback for the exercise. The application must already be able to start under the reduced capabilities; inspect failures rather than adding privileges until it runs. A read-only root filesystem can be added after identifying and providing the base image’s legitimate temporary write paths. (R56)

Linux example — 26.9

Run the lab image built in this chapter.

What to check: --rm removes this container on exit; it does not remove the image or external volumes.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.9 Running Containers

25. 26.10 Volumes

Volumes and bind mounts provide runtime data outside the container’s disposable writable layer. A named volume is managed by the runtime; a bind mount exposes a specified host path. Both require backup ownership and an access policy.

A read-only bind mount can protect release content from container writes. On SELinux hosts, relabel options such as :Z and :z have distinct private-versus-shared intent and can change labels on host content. Never apply them casually to broad system directories or a home directory containing unrelated data.

User-namespace mapping also affects ownership. Do not recursively change host ownership to a guessed container UID. Inspect the mapping and use the runtime’s supported tools on a dedicated data tree. (R56)

Linux example — 26.10

List and inspect a chosen lab volume.

What to check: Volume lifecycle and backup are separate from container lifecycle.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.10 Volumes

27. 26.11 Container Networking

A container can have its own network namespace with a private address and a runtime-managed path to the host or outside network. Port publishing connects a host listener to a container port under the chosen runtime’s implementation.

Test three different claims: the application listens inside; the host mapping reaches it; and an authorized external client can reach the host policy. A container’s loopback address is not the host’s loopback address.

Rootless networking can use user-space components whose behavior differs from rootful bridges. DNS, source-address presentation, and host reachability depend on the selected backend and version. Inspect effective configuration rather than transferring assumptions between engines.

Linux example — 26.11

Inspect container networks.

What to check: A rootless setup may use a different network name or backend; select an actual listed network.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.11 Container Networking

29. 26.12 Rootless Containers

Rootless containers run under an ordinary host account with user-namespace and related facilities rather than granting the runtime full host root by default. This reduces some consequences of runtime compromise, but it does not make exposed user files or credentials safe automatically.

Check subordinate UID/GID allocation, storage support, cgroup delegation, networking, and low-port restrictions under the installed distribution. A rootless service commonly uses a high application port behind a controlled proxy.

For persistent user services, the user’s systemd manager and optional lingering determine operation without an interactive login. Enabling lingering is an administrative lifecycle choice: the account can retain running services after logout. Record ownership and offboarding behavior.

Linux example — 26.12

Inspect rootless operation as an ordinary user.

What to check: Confirm rootless in the output; host user mappings still influence mounted-file permissions.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.12 Rootless Containers

31. 26.13 Container Security

Reduce the image to needed software, run with an appropriate non-root identity, remove unnecessary capabilities, avoid privileged mode, limit mounts, and restrict network paths. Retain host SELinux or AppArmor and the runtime’s applicable syscall filtering.

The container runtime socket is a sensitive control interface, not a routine application volume. Mounting it into a web application can expose the host’s orchestration powers. Similarly, a read-only image does not protect data on a separately writable host mount.

Patch both image and host. Rebuilding an image is not deployment, and deployment is not verification that all old instances are gone. Track the exact running artifact and test that rollback remains compatible with retained data.

Linux example — 26.13

Inspect a container's privilege and mount configuration.

What to check: Review capabilities, privileged mode, user, mounts, and exposed ports as separate controls.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.13 Container Security

33. 26.14 systemd and Containers

On supported Podman versions, Quadlet converts declarative files such as .container into systemd services. For rootless operation, a common source location is ~/.config/containers/systemd/. A minimal teaching file is:

After stopping the earlier standalone container to release its port, reload the user manager with systemctl --user daemon-reload and start the generated harbor-status.service for a file named harbor-status.container. Inspect generation errors and the installed manual if the service is missing. Quadlet’s generated services are not enabled like ordinary persistent unit files; the source file’s [Install] section establishes the generated activation relationship. Quadlet requires cgroup v2 in the referenced documentation. (R56)

Linux example — 26.14

Inspect user-level services that manage containers.

What to check: Quadlet availability depends on the installed Podman version and generator.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.14 systemd and Containers

36. 26.15 Troubleshooting Containers

Inspect the exit status, logs, effective configuration, mounts, resource events, and port mappings. A container that exits immediately may have completed its command correctly or failed before the application started.

Inspection can reveal environment secrets, so keep output protected. Do not debug by adding --privileged as a permanent fix. Determine whether the fault concerns identity, paths, unsupported architecture, missing dependencies, resource policy, or networking.

A manual exec repair inside a running container is usually temporary drift. Reproduce the correction in the image or declared runtime configuration, rebuild, and replace through a tested deployment process.

Linux example — 26.15

Read a bounded lab-container log.

What to check: Correlate exit status with logs and health checks; a running container may still serve a broken application.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — 26.15 Troubleshooting Containers

39. Requirement and preconditions

Use rootless Podman in an isolated Linux lab. The operator supplies a reviewed NGINX-compatible base image, pinned to an approved digest and confirmed to run as non-root on port 8080 with content under /usr/share/nginx/html. No registry account or digest is invented by the book.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — Requirement and preconditions

42. Demonstrate reproducibility

Stop and remove only the named lab container, then run a fresh one from the same recorded image with the same runtime settings. The response should contain the same marker without a manual edit inside the container. That demonstrates a narrow property: this release content is in the image rather than only in an abandoned writable layer.

Do not add volume-removal flags unless the lab explicitly created and owns those volumes. Transition to the Quadlet exercise only after releasing the host port; otherwise a port conflict obscures the supervision lesson.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — Demonstrate reproducibility

43. Demonstrate reproducibility · example 1

Stop and remove only the named lab container, then run a fresh one from the same recorded image with the same runtime settings. The response should contain the same marker without a manual edit inside the container. That demonstrates a narrow property: this release content is in the image rather than only in an abandoned writable layer.

Do not add volume-removal flags unless the lab explicitly created and owns those volumes. Transition to the Quadlet exercise only after releasing the host port; otherwise a port conflict obscures the supervision lesson.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — Demonstrate reproducibility

44. Recovery boundary

The image can recreate application files, but registry loss, host loss, secrets, and persistent data still need plans. Record those boundaries and verify the exact image under the selected systemd lifecycle before declaring the container operationally managed.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — Recovery boundary

45. Practice and implementation lab

Explain the difference between an image tag, image digest, running container, and persistent volume. Change a harmless file only inside a disposable container, replace the container, and observe whether the change survives. Do not use business data for this demonstration.

Check your understanding. Is container root always equivalent to host root? Its effect depends on mappings and privileges. Is it always harmless? No. Does a digest prove security? No. Can root and an ordinary user have different Podman inventories? Yes.

Chapter takeaway. Containers make packaging repeatable only when image identity, runtime policy, persistent data, and supervision are explicit.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch028.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

46. Preserve data outside an ephemeral runtime directory

Temporary directories model the storage distinction; this does not attest container isolation. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Preserve data outside an ephemeral runtime directory
